analysis.one_liner: Lets the President or a governor waive air-pollution and siting rules for fossil fuel power plants during declared electricity shortages.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced during the 2001 California power crisis with no cosponsors, died in committee and never received a vote before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, introduced during the California electricity crisis of 2001, would have let the President — or a governor the President authorizes — suspend Clean Air Act limits on how much or how long fossil fuel power plants can run, and waive federal siting rules under the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the Clean Water Act for new plants. It would also have barred the EPA from disapproving a state's air plan even if pollution from waived facilities pushed the state above federal air quality standards. A suspension would last as long as the President judged necessary to protect public health and safety.
analysis.who_benefits: Operators of fossil fuel fired power plants gain the most: during a declared electricity shortage they could run plants past Clean Air Act limits without facing EPA enforcement, and new plants could be sited without full environmental review under NEPA, the Endangered Species Act, or the Clean Water Act. The waiver's duration is left to the President's judgment.

how_it_helps.text: Allows the President to suspend Clean Air Act state implementation plan requirements that limit how long or how much a fossil fuel plant may generate during an electricity emergency [S2] [S3].

Allows suspension of siting requirements for new fossil fuel plants under the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act, and any federal, state, or local siting rules [S2] [S3].

Bars the EPA from disapproving a state's air quality plan, or imposing a federal replacement plan, even when emissions from waived facilities cause the state to exceed national ambient air quality standards [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People living near fossil fuel plants would breathe additional pollution during waivers, and the bill would shield those emissions even when they push air above federal health standards. Communities and habitats near proposed plant sites would lose the environmental and species review that normally applies to new construction. Because a waiver lasts as long as the President deems necessary, the duration of those costs is open-ended.
analysis.who_pays_short: People near plants and affected habitats

drawbacks.text: Waived emissions could push a state's air above national ambient air quality standards and the EPA would still be barred from disapproving the state's plan, removing a standard federal backstop [S3].
The suspension lasts for whatever period the President deems necessary, so an emergency designation could keep environmental requirements suspended indefinitely with no endpoint set in the bill [S3].
Waiving Endangered Species Act and Clean Water Act siting requirements for new plants would allow construction without the review that normally protects habitats and waterways [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real argument for fast emergency authority when a power shortage threatens public health and safety. But this bill goes beyond a narrow emergency tool: it waives Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, NEPA, and Endangered Species Act requirements on the President's own determination, allows waivers to continue for as long as the President deems necessary, and even blocks EPA from fixing a state air plan that becomes noncompliant because of waived emissions. The public health costs of added pollution and unreviewed siting outweigh the narrow reliability benefit, and no committee or member other than the sponsor supported it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then three subcommittees in March 2001, and none of them ever acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Duncan Hunter introduced the bill on March 13, 2001, with no cosponsors [S1] [S4] [S5].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees the day it was introduced [S5].
Within days it was sent to the Water Resources and Environment, Highways and Transit, and Energy and Air Quality subcommittees, where it remained [S5].
No committee ever voted on it, the House never took it up, and the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 without any further action [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody gained new authority: the bill died without a vote, so existing Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, and Endangered Species Act protections for power plant emissions and siting stayed fully in force. Communities near power plants are better off than they would have been under the bill, and no operator obtained any waiver authority from it.

for.name: Rep. Duncan Hunter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in March 2001 during the California electricity crisis; it attracted no cosponsors

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill sat in subcommittee for the rest of the Congress

against.name: House Natural Resources and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after their initial referrals

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill had a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and died in committee, so the partisan shape of potential support was never tested.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel fired electric power plants (coal, oil, gas)
industries.note: The bill would have let these operators run past Clean Air Act limits and site new plants without NEPA, Endangered Species Act, or Clean Water Act review during declared shortages. Because the bill died, they gained nothing; had it passed, their gains would have come at the cost of added air pollution near plants. It never advanced, so the industry's position was unchanged.

industries.industry: Coal-fired power plant construction and siting
industries.note: New fossil plant developers would have been able to bypass federal environmental siting review during emergencies, lowering their project costs and delays. The bill's failure left those review requirements intact.
